catalog_quote: Table 4 summarises the placement of stress in words with emphasis on different syllables according to the number of syllables. Stressed vowels appear in boldface type. Table 4: Pronunciation of and stress on different syllables | Number of Syllables | Stress | Duplication of syllables | One | gom, ram | fur-eran/furufur - eran | With two vowels | aidz, aom, Aus | Two | abang, ampat, angra boman, fofon, dare, fose, Yangka | abuabu | Three | Adanta, Adzimba, aposter, Aratsets, aetsantson, foarim, foareng | Two final vowels | fafoa | Four | Afoareng, abaeb-eran ... Dzob Wampar has not yet been systematically and comprehensively described and analysed ... As the present authors are anthropologists and not linguists, the following sections can only present a sketch of some features of the grammar

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place (PDF/printed p.13, Table 4 and the '5 Grammar sketch' opening); bold-vowel extraction in matches the record's the primary-stress rule. (2) The deciding source is a 2021 dictionary introduction by anthropologists that shows stress only by boldface on ~25 example words and states no rule; it is nevertheless the best published description: Glottolog's only other phonology-tagged work, Holzknecht 1989 (held, re-read pp.55-56), gives a Wampar phoneme table with no stress statement, and Crossref/ANU Press turn up nothing further. (3) Only unpublished manuscripts (Holzknecht 1998 ms sketch; Stuerzenhofecker 1930 ms) could improve the record; neither is obtainable online. (4) not determinable is an honest source-stated coding: the examples are consistent with penultimate stress on the stem (8/8 disyllables initial, 7/7 trisyllables penult
